design_detail: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (including randomised cross-over trials) of oral nicotine pouches given to people who used tobacco or other non-pharmaceutical nicotine products, to help them cut down or stop; a second arm of the question, population-level time-series studies of pouch uptake and the prevalence of smoking or other product use, found no eligible study. Critical outcomes: smoking abstinence at four weeks or longer (strictest definition, missing counted as smoking), serious adverse events at one week or longer, and smoking prevalence; important outcomes included adverse events, tobacco-specific nitrosamines (NNAL), carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb), metals and inflammatory markers. Random-effects pooling was planned but nearly every comparison rests on one trial, so the review mostly reports single-trial risk ratios and mean differences; one two-trial pool exists (NNAL, higher against lower dose). Three summary-of-findings tables with GRADE ratings (pouches against minimal control, against nicotine replacement therapy, against e-cigarettes). Four small trials, 284 participants, searched to 13 January 2025; ten further trials are listed as ongoing. Risk of bias (Cochrane RoB 1 tool): three trials high, one unclear, none low.
can_establish: What the randomised evidence available by January 2025 contained on nicotine pouches as an aid to cutting down or stopping smoking: four small, short trials (7 days to 8 weeks) with between 0 and 4 people quitting in any arm of the trials that reported quitting, no serious adverse events recorded in any arm, and short-term biomarker differences from single trials. The review shows how thin the evidence was at that date.
cannot_establish: Whether nicotine pouches help people stop smoking (the comparison with continued smoking rests on 1 quit among 18 people against 0 among 9); how they compare with nicotine replacement therapy (no cessation or serious-event data for that comparison) or with e-cigarettes beyond one trial with 5 quits in all; effects beyond 8 weeks; effects on people who vape or use other products (all participants smoked); how often serious harms occur (no events in any arm of three small, short trials); effects on prevalence of smoking or other nicotine use (no study); effects of pouches bought by people outside trials; and anything about trials that reported after the January 2025 search, including the ten ongoing trials.

sample.recruitment: CENTRAL (2025 issue 1), MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO from 2000 to 13 January 2025, with ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO trials platform through CENTRAL; no language limit; experts contacted and reference lists checked; industry publications such as shareholder reports were not searched. The search found 1,476 records (488 unique), 29 full texts, 4 included trials (14 records), 15 excluded and 10 ongoing; the authors of two included trials (Avila 2024; NCT04250727) were contacted and replied (Methods › Search methods; Results › Results of the search). Three trials were in the USA and one in New Zealand. Search strategies and the characteristics of each trial are in supplements that were not opened.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: individual or cluster randomised trials and randomised cross-over trials in people currently using any tobacco or non-pharmaceutical nicotine product (not only pouches), of pouches given to help them cut down or stop, with tobacco or nicotine use at four weeks or longer, or biomarkers or adverse events at one week or longer. Time-series studies were sought for population-level prevalence and none was found. Excluded: quasi-randomised studies; 15 studies excluded at full text (8 ineligible outcomes, 4 ineligible intervention, 1 ineligible design, 1 duplicate, 1 observational study with no population-level analysis).
sample.demographics: Adults who smoked cigarettes at baseline in all four trials (average age 34 to 50 in the plain language summary; 14 to 23 cigarettes a day; mostly white in the trials that reported ethnicity). Three trials enrolled people not planning to quit; one (Caldwell 2010) included some people strongly interested in quitting or cutting down. At least three trials excluded people with recent use of other tobacco or nicotine products, pouches included, so most participants had not used pouches before. Three trials were in people aged over 21; the age cut-off of the fourth is unclear.
sample.attrition: Cessation was analysed with missing counted as smoking; other outcomes were complete-case, so cigarettes per day among people who kept smoking rest on 19 of 27 and 26 of 36 people. The review rated attrition and selective reporting low risk in all four trials. Avila 2024's registry lists cotinine, NNAL and 8-isoprostane, which were not analysed for lack of funding; the review says it does not treat this as a risk of bias.
sample.selection_effects: Four small trials of people who volunteered, 30 to 146 each. Two trials told people to use the product when they wanted to smoke rather than to quit, one told people to stop their usual brand (Rensch 2023), and three enrolled people not planning to quit, so quitting was not what most participants were asked to do. Products were supplied free. Only the tobacco-industry trial (Rensch 2023) contributes most of the biomarker data against continued smoking. The review was commissioned within an NIH and FDA tobacco regulatory science centre (CAsToR 3.0) whose steering committee commented on scope but, the review says, could not decide whether it is published or what it finds.

exposure.measurement: Allocation in the trial to pouches, or to a comparison product. Products named: nicotine pouches (2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 mg; original, mint and other flavours; brands include On!, Zyn and Zonnic), e-cigarette pods with 5% nicotine in tobacco or menthol flavour, snus (8 mg) and nicotine gum (4 mg). Product use was recorded in some trials (for example willingness to continue pouch use in NCT04250727); adherence was not synthesised.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as reported, not recommendations: Avila 2024 supplied products for four weeks with a choice of flavour and followed people to week 8; NCT04250727 supplied Zyn 3 mg or 6 mg, eight cans a week for four weeks, with a weekly check-in phone call; Rensch 2023 gave On! 2, 4 or 8 mg as much as wanted apart from three test-use occasions on the study day, with biomarkers at about day 7, against a no-tobacco group and a continue-smoking group; Caldwell 2010 was a cross-over of three products in random order. Follow-up across the four trials ran from 7 days to 8 weeks. In two trials people were told to use the product when they wanted to smoke.
exposure.polysubstance: At least three trials excluded recent use of tobacco or nicotine products other than cigarettes. Dual use of cigarettes and pouches occurred: two people in the 6 mg arm of NCT04250727 reported symptoms they or the investigators attributed to nicotine toxicity during dual use (one paused and resumed pouches; one stopped and withdrew).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Avila 2024: cigarette abstinence at week 8 (biochemically validated per the summary-of-findings table); NCT04250727: abstinence at week 4, carbon monoxide below 5 ppm. Rensch 2023 and Caldwell 2010 reported no smoking outcome.

comparison.controls: Minimal control (continue smoking as usual or no intervention: Avila 2024, 9 people; Rensch 2023), an e-cigarette (Avila 2024), a no-tobacco group (Rensch 2023), snus and 4 mg nicotine gum (Caldwell 2010, cross-over), and a lower-dose pouch (NCT04250727; Rensch 2023).
comparison.matching: Selection bias: low risk in Avila 2024, unclear in the other three (randomisation or concealment not described). Performance bias: low in Caldwell 2010, high in Avila 2024 and Rensch 2023 (unblinded, different levels of intervention), unclear in NCT04250727 (registry entry only). Detection bias: low in three (biochemical validation), high in Caldwell 2010 (no objective outcomes). Attrition, selective reporting and other bias: rated low in all four.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not examined; planned subgroups (flavour, nicotine dose, intensity of support) and sensitivity analyses (high risk of bias, industry funding) were precluded because no pool had more than two trials; the review notes only that the NNAL dose result did not change when the one high-risk, industry-funded trial was removed.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Use of other products outside the study was exclusionary at entry in at least three trials; use during the study was not synthesised. Comparisons between pouches and NRT or snus come from one cross-over trial with adverse-event outcomes only.

outcomes.instruments: Smoking abstinence at 4+ weeks (carbon monoxide validated where reported); serious and other adverse events at 1+ weeks, collected by self-report, a respiratory questionnaire (Avila 2024), Likert-scale side-effect ratings (Caldwell 2010), a registry list (NCT04250727) or a narrative report (Rensch 2023); NNAL and COHb plus 16 further urinary biomarkers in Rensch 2023; exhaled carbon monoxide in Avila 2024; cigarettes per day.
outcomes.validity_norms: Adverse events were recorded in four different ways and could not be pooled. Rensch 2023 gave a narrative report not split by arm: 56 of 146 people (38%) had 86 events, 76 mild and 10 moderate, headache most common (23 people), and 4 events judged related to the product. Rensch 2023 supplied 18 analysed biomarkers (NNAL, COHb and 16 others); Table 4 also lists nicotine equivalents and urine mutagenicity, which no analysis reports.
outcomes.operationalization: Quit = strictest abstinence definition at the longest follow-up of 4 weeks or more, missing counted as smoking. Serious adverse events = potentially life-threatening, needing hospital care, or causing disability or death; other medical problems (cough, headache, dry mouth) counted as adverse events. Each biomarker analysed separately, complete case. Zero-event cells handled by a 0.5 correction, which gives the printed risk ratio for 1 of 18 against 0 of 9.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Six outcomes per summary-of-findings table; Rensch 2023 alone supplied 18 biomarkers, each reported with an unadjusted 95% interval, and the text lists which favoured which arm.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Review authors screened and extracted data in duplicate and assessed risk of bias in duplicate, and were not blinded to trial results. Within trials, detection bias was rated low in three of four trials because key outcomes were biochemically validated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Smoking abstinence (random-effects methods planned, single-trial risk ratios reported): pouch against minimal control at week 8, 1 of 18 against 0 of 9, RR 1.58 (95% CI 0.07 to 35.32), 27 participants, very low certainty (summary-of-findings table: 11 per 1,000 with minimal control against 18 per 1,000, interval 1 to 392; the control figure comes from the zero-event correction, since no control participant quit); pouch against e-cigarette at week 8, 1 of 18 against 4 of 18, RR 0.25 (0.03 to 2.02), 36 participants, 222 against 56 per 1,000 (7 to 449), low certainty; 6 mg against 3 mg pouch at week 4, 2 of 15 against 0 of 15, RR 5.00 (0.26 to 96.13), 30 participants, certainty not assessed. Cigarettes per day among people still smoking: against minimal control MD -1.07 (-12.72 to 10.58), n = 19; against e-cigarette MD 5.32 (-2.16 to 12.80), n = 26; 6 mg against 3 mg, log-scale MD -0.20 (-0.27 to -0.13), n = 30. Serious adverse events: none in any arm (against minimal control 2 trials, 124 participants, very low; against e-cigarette 1 trial, 26, low; higher against lower dose 2 trials, 77). Any adverse event, 6 mg against 3 mg: 13 of 15 in each arm, RR 1.00 (0.76 to 1.32). Biomarkers against minimal control (Rensch 2023, 53 people, one week): NNAL MD -265.30 ng/g creatinine (-350.64 to -179.96), control mean 330; COHb MD -6.7% (-8.33 to -5.07), control mean 11.3%, very low certainty; 16 further biomarkers all favoured pouches with intervals excluding no difference. Against a no-tobacco group (Rensch 2023, 46 people): none of 18 biomarkers clearly differed. Higher against lower dose: NNAL SMD -0.16 (-1.87 to 1.56), I2 0%, 2 trials, 77 participants; COHb MD -0.40% (-1.19 to 0.39).
analysis.covariates: None. Planned subgroups by flavour, nicotine dose, support intensity and analysis type were precluded by too few studies.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Cochrane protocol (published Issue 2, 2025; DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD016220), cited as the registration. The page has no section listing differences from the protocol and the protocol was not opened, so deviations, if any, cannot be listed; the Methods state which planned analyses (random-effects pooling, subgroups, sensitivity analyses, funnel plots, ROBINS-I, time-series synthesis) could not be done.
analysis.selective_reporting: The review rated selective reporting low risk in all four trials, and says Avila 2024's unreported registry biomarkers were not analysed for lack of funding; the Cochrane e-cigarette living review rates the same trial high risk for possible selective reporting for the same reason. The review notes that NCT04250727 is a registry record without a publication.
analysis.power: At most two trials contributed to any analysis and most outcomes had one or none. Events: 1 quitter among 27 people against minimal control; 5 quitters among 36 against the e-cigarette; 2 quitters among 30 for the dose comparison; no serious event in any arm. Every outcome carries serious imprecision.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Four small trials (284 people, 7 days to 8 weeks) are the whole randomised evidence in this review. Quitting smoking was reported by two trials: 1 of 18 people given pouches had quit at week 8 against 0 of 9 who were left to smoke as usual (RR 1.58, 0.07 to 35.32; very low certainty), and 1 of 18 against 4 of 18 given e-cigarettes (RR 0.25, 0.03 to 2.02; low certainty; about 17 fewer in 100 on the point estimate, interval from about 22 fewer to 23 more in 100 on the summary-of-findings figures); a third trial found 2 of 15 quitting at 6 mg against 0 of 15 at 3 mg at week 4 (RR 5.00, 0.26 to 96.13). None of these differences is distinguishable from chance. No serious adverse events were recorded in any arm of three trials, and other adverse events were reported in different ways (cough and breathlessness more often with pouches than e-cigarettes in the first week and similar by week four; 38% of the 146 people in Rensch 2023 had an event, mostly mild). Biomarker differences from single trials after about one week of use pointed lower with pouches than with continued smoking (NNAL 330 against about 65 ng/g creatinine implied; COHb 11.3% against about 4.6% implied, editors' arithmetic), with very low certainty, one of them from the tobacco-industry trial; 18 biomarkers against a no-tobacco group showed no clear difference. There is no randomised evidence on pouches against NRT for quitting, on people who vape, on follow-up beyond eight weeks, or on prevalence.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says smoking abstinence may be slightly higher with pouches than no intervention and that people on pouches may be slightly less likely to quit than people on e-cigarettes; the conclusions say limited, short-term data did not identify serious health harms; the plain language summary says its key finding is no short-term serious health harms in three small studies, and that it was unclear whether pouches helped people quit relative to continuing as usual. Gaps: (1) 'may be slightly higher' rests on one person quitting among 18 against none among 9, with an interval from 0.07 to 35.32, which cannot show higher or lower; the summary-of-findings control risk (11 per 1,000) is an artefact of the zero-event correction; (2) 'slightly less likely' than e-cigarettes describes 1 against 4 quitters, a point estimate of 17 fewer in 100 with an interval that spans a large difference either way, from one unblinded trial; (3) the plain language summary says two small studies underlie the comparisons with continued smoking and with e-cigarettes, but both come from one trial (Avila 2024); (4) the key message that no short-term serious health harms were found is a statement about absence of recorded events in three small studies over 1 to 8 weeks, which the same summary says leaves it unclear whether serious harm is affected; (5) the Results outcomes paragraph says two trials reported serious events while the abstract and conclusions say three; (6) the review says the industry-funded trial's findings were consistent with independent trials, yet it is the only trial of NNAL and COHb against continued smoking, so no independent comparison exists for those outcomes; (7) the risk-of-bias text says all expected outcomes were reported while noting that Avila 2024 did not report registry-listed biomarkers.

timeline.event: This review published in October 2025; search to 13 January 2025; four trials included and ten listed as ongoing; the authors say they know of no other systematic review with similar objectives.

The Cochrane living review of e-cigarettes for smoking cessation (search to January 2026) includes the same Avila 2024 trial as its only nicotine pouch comparison, with no cessation result for pouches.

replication.where_it_stands: Nothing here has been replicated: each quit result comes from one trial of 27 to 36 people (or 30 for the dose comparison), and the biomarker findings against continued smoking come from one industry-funded trial. The review states its own limits plainly (serious imprecision for every outcome, at most two trials per analysis) and lists ten ongoing trials. Trials completed after the January 2025 search, and the ongoing trials, are not covered here.

funding.funder: National Cancer Institute of the US National Institutes of Health and the FDA Center for Tobacco Products (award 2U54CA229974), through the Center for the Assessment of Tobacco Regulation (CAsToR 3.0), which commissioned the review; the funders were not involved in the decision to submit for publication. No internal sources of support are listed. Of the four included trials, three were funded by philanthropic, academic or governmental bodies and one (Rensch 2023) by the manufacturer of the pouch tested (a tobacco company); the review says no review author was involved in any included trial.
funding.declared_conflicts: Review authors declare: payments from the Truth Initiative and the US FDA and grants from NIH, FDA, WHO and others (JHB); unpaid membership of the advisory board of a smoking cessation app (JB); honoraria, an unrestricted grant and travel from Pfizer and a panel honorarium from Johnson and Johnson, both makers of smoking cessation medicines (LS); a Pfizer research grant and membership of a Johnson and Johnson scientific advisory board, and consulting for the FDA, WHO and others on tobacco product toxicity (MLG); lecture payments and research grants from public and charity funders (NL); public grants and consultancy for the WHO (HJ). JHB, JB and JLB are Cochrane editors who took no part in the editorial process. No author declares funding from a tobacco, nicotine pouch or e-cigarette company (LS states he has never received any from alcohol, e-cigarette or tobacco companies). HTB, CLM, ADW and NT declare no conflicts. Two people with lived experience of pouches gave feedback on plans and write-up.
funding.affiliations_note: Author affiliations were not in the page text read for this card, apart from the declarations (University College London for JB; Cochrane roles).

what_would_settle_it: Adequately sized randomised trials of nicotine pouches against nicotine replacement therapy and nicotine vapes in people trying to stop smoking, with carbon monoxide or cotinine validated abstinence at six months or longer, serious adverse events and the amount of pouch use after quitting followed for as long as possible, registered outcomes, and funding independent of pouch makers; results from the ten ongoing trials; biomarker trials longer than a week and from more than one funder; and separate population-level work on uptake by people who never smoked, which these trials cannot address.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: People using tobacco or other non-pharmaceutical nicotine products; oral nicotine pouches; comparators listed (other products, other pouch doses, medicines, placebo pouches, very low nicotine cigarettes, minimal control); smoking abstinence, serious adverse events and prevalence as critical outcomes; randomised trials and, for prevalence, time-series studies.

A Cochrane protocol (Issue 2, 2025) is cited as the registration and the Methods follow it by design; the page has no section on differences from the protocol and the protocol was not opened, so deviations cannot be checked.
Randomised, cluster-randomised and cross-over trials for benefits and harms (quasi-randomised excluded) and time-series studies for prevalence, with the reason for each stated.

Four databases and two registries to January 2025 with no language limit, experts contacted, reference lists checked, search strategy by an information specialist in a supplement (not opened); industry publications were not searched, and the authors say eligible trials may have been missed.
Two review authors independently screened titles, abstracts and full texts.
Two authors independently extracted outcome data and risk of bias information; study characteristics were extracted by one author.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The 15 studies excluded at full text are listed in a supplement with reasons (the duplicate excluded from that list).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 4 and the text give country, arms, outcomes, risk of bias, participants, products and nicotine content, instructions, duration and follow-up for each of the four trials; full characteristics sit in a supplement that was not opened.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane RoB 1 tool (selection, performance, detection, attrition, selective reporting, other) by two independent assessors on the critical outcomes only; the selective-reporting rating for Avila 2024 is arguable (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Funding and author conflicts were extracted verbatim; the page states which trial was funded by a tobacco manufacturer and that the other three had independent funders (names are in the supplement).

Pooled only trials with the same comparator and outcome; one two-trial pool (NNAL) by generic inverse-variance random effects; single-trial risk ratios with a zero-cell correction; planned Mantel-Haenszel pooling was not possible. Almost all results are single-trial figures.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses could not be done; for the one pool the text says the NNAL result did not change when the single high-risk, industry-funded trial was removed.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: GRADE downgraded for risk of bias and imprecision (very low for comparison with minimal control) and the Discussion states the limits; the abstract wording on direction of effect goes beyond what the certainty ratings support.
I2 0% for the single pool; the Methods set thresholds and state none was needed.
The review states there were too few studies for any formal assessment (no analysis pooled more than two trials); the ten ongoing trials are listed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Declarations for every author and the funder are given; no author was involved in an included trial.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No critical item is judged no; item 2 is only partly met, which AMSTAR 2 does not count as a flaw. AMSTAR 2 rates how the review was done, not how good its evidence is: here the evidence is four small trials, 284 people, one to eight weeks, three at high risk of bias, with at most two trials in any analysis and every outcome rated seriously imprecise. May be cited for: a plain statement that, by January 2025, randomised evidence on pouches for stopping smoking was one trial of 27 people against continued smoking and one of 36 against e-cigarettes, with 5 quitters in all, no recorded serious adverse events, and short-term biomarker differences from single trials. May not be cited for: any statement that pouches help or do not help people stop smoking, that they are or are not safe, or that they compare with NRT or vapes in effectiveness.

key_findings.finding: Included trials: four randomised trials, 284 participants (Avila 2024, USA, 45 people: pouch, e-cigarette, no intervention; Caldwell 2010, New Zealand, 63, cross-over of pouch, snus and 4 mg nicotine gum; NCT04250727, USA, 30: 6 mg against 3 mg Zyn pouches, registry record only; Rensch 2023, USA, 146, tobacco-industry funded: On! pouches of three strengths against a no-tobacco group and a continue-smoking group). All enrolled adults who smoked; three enrolled people not planning to quit; follow-up 7 days to 8 weeks. Ten ongoing trials are listed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Included studies, Table 4 (overview), Participants, Interventions and comparators; Results of the search

key_findings.finding: Pouch against minimal control (continue smoking as usual), abstinence at week 8: 1 of 18 people given pouches had quit against 0 of 9 with no intervention; RR 1.58 (95% CI 0.07 to 35.32), 1 trial, 27 participants (Avila 2024, high risk of bias). Very low certainty (downgraded two levels for risk of bias and two for imprecision). The summary-of-findings table prints 11 per 1,000 with no intervention and 18 per 1,000 with pouches (1 to 392), figures that come from the zero-event correction since no control participant quit. Among people who kept smoking, cigarettes per day at week 8: mean difference -1.07 (-12.72 to 10.58), 19 people with complete data (Avila 2024); the interval includes large differences in both directions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP versus minimal control › Smoking behaviour, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Summary of findings 1, row 1 and footnotes a and b
key_findings.note: The per-1,000 figures are not observed rates; the observed counts are 1 of 18 and 0 of 9.

key_findings.finding: Pouch against e-cigarette (5% nicotine pods), abstinence at week 8: 1 of 18 quit with pouches against 4 of 18 with e-cigarettes; RR 0.25 (0.03 to 2.02), 1 trial, 36 participants; 222 per 1,000 with e-cigarettes against 56 per 1,000 (7 to 449) with pouches, about 17 fewer in 100 on the point estimate (editors' subtraction). Low certainty (two levels for imprecision; 5 events in all); not downgraded for risk of bias because both arms were equally intensive although unblinded. Cigarettes per day among people still smoking: MD 5.32 (-2.16 to 12.80), 26 people with complete data; exhaled carbon monoxide higher with pouches, interval including no difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP versus e-cigarettes › Smoking behaviour and Biomarkers; Summary of findings 3

key_findings.finding: Higher against lower nicotine pouch (NCT04250727; registry record, unclear risk of bias), abstinence at week 4: 2 of 15 quit at 6 mg against 0 of 15 at 3 mg; RR 5.00 (0.26 to 96.13), 30 participants; certainty not assessed (a dose comparison was not a planned summary-of-findings comparison). Cigarettes per day (log scale) lower with 6 mg: MD -0.20 (-0.27 to -0.13), n = 30. Any adverse event 13 of 15 in each arm, RR 1.00 (0.76 to 1.32); two 6 mg participants reported nicotine toxicity symptoms during dual use of cigarettes and pouches.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP at different nicotine content doses › Smoking behaviour and Adverse events; Table 5 (NCT04250727)

key_findings.finding: Serious adverse events: none in any arm in the trials reporting them. Against minimal control, 2 trials (Avila 2024; Rensch 2023), 124 participants, very low certainty (two levels for risk of bias, two for imprecision); against e-cigarettes, 1 trial, 26 participants, low certainty (imprecision); higher against lower dose, NCT04250727 and Rensch 2023, 77 participants; against a no-tobacco group, Rensch 2023, none. Follow-up 1 to 8 weeks. The authors conclude it is unclear whether pouches change the chance of a serious event.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Adverse events (ONP against minimal control; ONP versus e-cigarettes; ONP at different doses); Summary of findings 1 and 3; Plain language summary › What did we find?

key_findings.finding: Other adverse events (not pooled; Table 5): cough and shortness of breath were more frequent with pouches than with e-cigarettes in the first week of Avila 2024 (cough 5 against 3, breathlessness 6 against 1 people) and similar by week 4; Rensch 2023 reported 86 events in 56 of 146 people (38%), 76 mild and 10 moderate, headache most frequent (23 people), 4 judged related to the product (2 headaches, 1 nausea, 1 mouth irritation), not split by arm; Caldwell 2010 (63 people, rating scales) found side effects uncommon for pouch, snus and gum, with fewer reports of bad taste with pouches than snus or gum, and discontinuation for gastrointestinal symptoms by 1 person on pouch, 2 on gum and 1 on snus.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Adverse events; ONP versus snus; ONP versus nicotine replacement therapy; Table 5

key_findings.finding: Biomarkers against minimal control (Rensch 2023, tobacco-industry funded, high risk, 53 people, about one week): NNAL MD -265.30 ng/g creatinine (-350.64 to -179.96) from a control mean of 330; COHb MD -6.7% (-8.33 to -5.07) from a control mean of 11.3%; 16 further urinary biomarkers all favoured pouches with intervals excluding no difference. Very low certainty (risk of bias, imprecision). Against a no-tobacco group (46 people) none of 18 biomarkers clearly differed. Avila 2024 (19 people) found lower exhaled carbon monoxide with pouches than continued smoking, interval including no difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP versus minimal control › Biomarkers; ONP versus no tobacco or nicotine product use › Biomarkers; Summary of findings 1, rows 3 and 4

key_findings.finding: Biomarkers, higher against lower dose: NNAL SMD -0.16 (-1.87 to 1.56), I2 0%, 2 trials (NCT04250727 and Rensch 2023), 77 participants, unchanged without Rensch 2023; COHb MD -0.40% (-1.19 to 0.39). Of 17 further biomarkers in Rensch 2023, point estimates for nine favoured the lower dose (intervals including no difference), four the higher dose, three the lower dose with intervals excluding no difference (HEMA, AAMA, GAMA) and one showed no difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › ONP at different nicotine content doses › Biomarkers

key_findings.finding: Gaps in the evidence, as the review states: no study of prevalence of smoking or other nicotine use; no data on pouches for stopping or cutting down vaping, heated tobacco, snus or other products (all participants smoked); no data on metals or inflammatory markers; no trial with follow-up beyond 8 weeks; no abstinence result for the comparison with NRT; at most two studies in any analysis, so serious imprecision for every outcome; ten ongoing studies; industry publications not searched.
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of studies › Outcomes; Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review; Authors' conclusions

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias in the four trials: none low overall; Avila 2024, Caldwell 2010 and Rensch 2023 high, NCT04250727 unclear. Selection bias low in Avila 2024, unclear in the others; performance bias high in Avila 2024 and Rensch 2023 (unblinded, unequal intervention), low in Caldwell 2010, unclear in NCT04250727; detection bias low in three, high in Caldwell 2010; attrition, selective reporting and other bias low in all four.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 1st to 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Funding: Rensch 2023 was funded by the pouch manufacturer (a tobacco company); the other three trials by philanthropic, academic or governmental bodies. The industry trial reported no smoking outcome, no serious events, and the largest set of biomarker results. The review was funded by the US National Cancer Institute and FDA Center for Tobacco Products through CAsToR 3.0. The review says no author took part in an included trial.
key_findings.locator: Results › Included studies › Funding; Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review, 2nd paragraph; Sources of support; Declarations of interest

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: eligible trials may have been missed through indexing or terminology; intention-to-treat with missing counted as smoking may underestimate absolute quit rates; other outcomes were complete case; industry reports were not searched; evidence reaches January 2025; future trials should compare pouches with NRT and nicotine e-cigarettes and measure abstinence and serious events as long as possible, ideally at six months or longer.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations of the review processes; Authors' conclusions › Implications for research

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says smoking abstinence may be slightly higher with pouches than no intervention. The data are one person who quit among 18 given pouches and none among 9 left to smoke (RR 1.58, 0.07 to 35.32); an interval this wide cannot show higher or lower. The summary-of-findings table prints a control risk of 11 per 1,000 although no control participant quit.
reporting_issues.locator: Abstract › Synthesis of results, Smoking abstinence; Summary of findings 1, row 1; Results › ONP versus minimal control › Smoking behaviour
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim reports the counts (1 of 18, 0 of 9) and states that the result is not informative.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and conclusions say people given pouches may be slightly less likely to quit than people given e-cigarettes. The data are 1 of 18 against 4 of 18 (RR 0.25, 0.03 to 2.02; 5 events, one unblinded trial); the table's own absolute figures (56 against 222 per 1,000) are not slight, and the interval spans a large difference either way.
reporting_issues.locator: Abstract › Authors' conclusions; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice, 3rd paragraph; Summary of findings 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim reports the counts and the interval and does not use 'slightly'.

reporting_issues.issue: The plain language summary says its statement on quitting rests on two small studies; the comparisons with continued smoking and with e-cigarettes both come from one trial (Avila 2024), and the other trial that reported quitting (NCT04250727) compared two pouch strengths.
reporting_issues.locator: Plain language summary › What did we find?, 4th paragraph; Results › Outcomes
reporting_issues.consequence: One trial per comparison is used.

reporting_issues.issue: The key message in the plain language summary says no short-term serious health harms were found, while the same summary says it is unclear whether pouches change the chance of a serious event. The record is no serious event in any arm of three small trials lasting 1 to 8 weeks.
reporting_issues.locator: Plain language summary › Key messages and What did we find?
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim states no serious events were recorded and that the data cannot show frequency.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of trials reporting serious adverse events is two in the Outcomes paragraph (Avila 2024; Rensch 2023) but three in the abstract and conclusions and in the dose comparison, which includes NCT04250727; Table 4 lists no serious-event outcome for NCT04250727.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Outcomes, 'Of the critical outcomes'; Abstract › Synthesis of results; Results › ONP at different nicotine content doses › Adverse events; Table 4
reporting_issues.consequence: Three trials with serious-event data is used, as in the abstract and the dose comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: The review rates selective reporting low for Avila 2024 and says all expected outcomes were reported, while noting in the same paragraph and in Table 4 that biomarkers listed on the trial registry (cotinine, NNAL, 8-isoprostane) were not reported; the Cochrane e-cigarette review rates the same trial high risk of bias for selective reporting for the same reason.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies › Incomplete outcome data and selective reporting; Table 4 (Avila 2024)
reporting_issues.consequence: Flagged; the overall high risk for the trial does not change.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says the industry-funded trial's findings were consistent with independent trials, but Rensch 2023 is the only trial reporting NNAL and COHb against continued smoking, so no independent trial exists to compare for those outcomes.
reporting_issues.locator: Discussion › Limitations of the evidence included in the review, 2nd paragraph; Results › ONP versus minimal control › Biomarkers
reporting_issues.consequence: Funding is reported beside the biomarker result; the consistency statement is not repeated.

reporting_issues.issue: Number and label slips: the adverse-event comparison for NCT04250727 is given as n = 15 where each arm has 15 (30 in all); Table 5 labels the 6 mg arm '5mg' in two rows; summary-of-findings comments label mean differences 'RR for 1 study'; 2-AN is expanded as 2-aminoadipic acid in the Results but 2-aminonaphthalene in Table 4; Table 4 lists nicotine equivalents and urine mutagenicity among Rensch 2023's outcomes but no analysis reports them; the Background gives the year of the US Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act as 2019 (the editors believe it is 2009 and have not checked); the Discussion refers to reviews of 'nicotine cigarettes' where e-cigarettes appear to be meant.
reporting_issues.locator: Results › ONP at different nicotine content doses › Adverse events; Table 5; Summary of findings 1, comments; Results › Included studies, Table 4; Background › Description of the intervention; Discussion › Agreements and disagreements with other studies or reviews
